Sports Investing Is for Millionaires Now, not Billionaires
 
Plus, oil’s up and everything else is down
 

When even Elon Musk’s techno-boosterism can’t get investors excited then you know the world is a troubled place. Tesla results, and a proposed megamerger, seem to matter less than rising oil prices and French bond yields. U.S. stock futures point to a down day—especially for the tech-heavy Nasdaq.

It’s Showtime

 

It sounds unbelievable now, but Jerry Buss bought the L.A. Lakers for just $67.5 million in 1979. Those assets sold at a $10 billion valuation last year, earning him posthumous accolades for the best sports investment ever.

 

Well, he did alright. Some teams were bought long before that for thousands or even just hundreds of dollars upfront, says Ron Diamond, who runs a syndicate of family offices. 

 

Since 1961, the Ross-Arctos Sports Franchise Index has compounded at about 13% versus around 10% for U.S. stocks, and it’s up 16% over the past decade (Buss made around 11.5% annually). A lot of those valuations stem from teams occasionally selling minority stakes in themselves to funds.

 

Such deals will get more common. Some 173 billionaire families own a piece of sports franchises. Diamond says most are poorly equipped to maintain family control given unwieldy ownership structures. Exhibit A is a less-glowing aspect of the Buss saga—the nasty legal battle among his heirs about whether to sell their remaining stake.

 

Enter family offices (sophisticated private funds for wealthy people) more interested in returns than hobnobbing with players. Bank of America’s private bank says four-in-ten family offices hold sports investments and that Gen Z and millennial principals are most likely to be interested.

 

There are a handful of North American teams open to the investing public such as Madison Square Garden Sports, Atlanta Braves Holdings and Rogers Communications. But the best returns may now be in less-known or glamorous corners of the $2.5 trillion market rather than in outright team control.

 

Minority positions, media rights, stadiums, lending, emerging leagues and college athletics offer less competition.

 

Sports is an investing rarity in being both safe and fast-growing. In a shifting media landscape, it’s hard to disrupt and in high demand since it’s one of the last things millions of people pay to watch simultaneously, and legalized sports betting has opened up new ways to profit.

 

Private equity has gotten in on the sports investing act too, as have Middle Eastern sovereign-wealth funds and royalty. The latter have concentrated on leagues outside North America, partly because of regulations.  

 

Some look undervalued given their global fan bases, but European soccer teams fetch less for a reason. Diamond notes that American sports franchises are “permanent, protected, revenue-shared monopoly licenses in a defined territory, sold once and never reissued.” Media sales are collective, salaries are somewhat controlled and losing teams don’t face relegation.

 

As founding families move on, a lot of money will be put to work by investors as excited by making a bundle as they are by the thrill of victory.

↘️ Tesla: Elon Musk’s EV company said it will spend about $20 billion in capital expenditures this year, less than an earlier estimate of $25 billion. Musk refused to discuss a possible merger with SpaceX on a call with analysts. Shares fell premarket.

 

↘️ Meta Platforms: The Facebook owner reported record revenue for the third quarter and said it would create a new class of nonvoting stock to raise capital for its AI mega-bet. Shares slipped premarket, having initially risen after yesterday’s close.

 

↘️ Nvidia, SpaceX, Micron: Some of the biggest names in artificial intelligence dropped premarket, the latest jitters to slow the AI trade that has dominated global stock markets.

 

↘️ Lam Research: Shares of the company, which makes chip-production equipment, dropped even though its revenue and adjusted profit topped analyst forecasts, a sign of lofty expectations for AI-related companies.
